title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
text:
Radiance Rules Update Effective October 16, 2026
Welcome to the patch notes for Riftbound, Radiance edition. Included in today’s update are rules for playing with Radiance’s new mechanics, updates from the Vendetta FAQ, improvements to the rules’ logical infrastructure to better prepare for future sets and mechanics and a collection of scenarios to help folks understand some of the more complicated interactions introduced with Radiance.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: Unique Radiance Interactions
text:
Unique Radiance Interactions
While the patch notes and core rules are aimed at arming our judges, we wanted to include questions and answers prepared by the design team for some of the more tricky interactions and cards released in that set. This article will be released in addition to an FAQ article in the window when we’ve previously released FAQ articles.
Although this article is not an FAQ, it still is a collection of official rulings. These rulings are based on the Core Rules Document that also releases today, as well as the wording of the cards. When a new version of the Core Rules Document is released, it will take precedence over any points that differ from this document.
Throughout this document, we use some specific shorthand to represent symbols in card text. Here’s a short guide:
[E] means “exhaust”
[M] means “Might”
[A] means “one power of any domain”
[C] means “one power of this card’s domain”[C] in Accelerate costs takes on the domain of the Unit, or turns into [A] if the Unit has no domain or multiple domains.[C] in other cases is treated as the corresponding power symbol in all respects, matching how the cards are actually printed—it’s just a design shorthand!

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: What happens when I play Ekko, Boy Who Shattered Time’s activated ability, play a unit, and then play Unlicensed Armoy’s activated ability? Will the unit be kil
text:
Q: What happens when I play Ekko, Boy Who Shattered Time’s activated ability, play a unit, and then play Unlicensed Armoy’s activated ability? Will the unit be killed on my next turn?
Your unit’s death from its triggered ability will be replaced by Unlicensed Armory. Although the unit has the text “Kill me at end of turn.” appended to it, that text is synonymous with “Kill me at the end of this turn.” On subsequent turns, it will not trigger.
When “at end of turn” appears on card text, it is used synonymously with “at the end of this turn.” Although granting that text to a unit is strange, it isn’t outside the bounds of possibility. If the unit remains on the board after the triggered ability resolves, the condition for its ability to trigger will no longer be able to be fulfilled, so it will not trigger again. If the unit changes zones to or from a non-board zone prior to the triggered ability triggering, all of its temporary modifications—including this granted text—will be removed. As such, the ability will no longer exist to trigger.
Relevant rules: 359.3.e.16., 124.1.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: Can I show off a facedown card at a battlefield with the Show Off ability of Gutter Guardian?
text:
Q: Can I show off a facedown card at a battlefield with the Show Off ability of Gutter Guardian?
You cannot. Facedown cards don’t have any referenceable characteristics from their front side.
The keyword “Hidden” only appears on the front side of the card; that’s the side with the cost, name, Might, and rules text among other traits. While a card is facedown, any information on its front side cannot be referenced by other cards and effects. Although a facedown card may be friendly to Gutter Guardian, it doesn’t have the appropriate characteristic to be shown off. Note that only the card from hand is revealed with Show Off. You don’t reveal the friendly objects on the board that you’re Showing Off, so you can’t reveal the facedown card even if you wanted to.
Relevant rules: 811.5.a., 129.4.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: What’s up with the reminder text on Chronobreak? Do I get to choose the order?
text:
Q: What’s up with the reminder text on Chronobreak? Do I get to choose the order?
You get to choose the order if you own all of the units being banished. If you control some number of units that you don’t own and banish those units as well, the units you banish will be placed on the chain starting with units owned by the current turn player and then proceeding in turn order.
Items cannot be placed on the chain simultaneously for any reason. If chain items would be played simultaneously, their controller chooses the order they go on the chain. If multiple players would add items to the chain simultaneously, they place their items on the chain in turn order instead, starting with the current turn player. In the case of Chronobreak, each player chooses the order of their own units being played to the chain (this is what the reminder text is referring to), but each player plays their units to the chain in turn order, starting with the current turn player.
Example: You control five total units, two of which are owned by your opponent. You play Chronobreak, choosing all five units. You banish them, then for each, their owner plays them to the chain as pending items. You’re the current turn player, so you play your three units first in the order of your choice, then your opponent plays their two units in the order of their choice. Pending chain items are finalized from oldest to newest and units resolve as soon as they’re finalized. Thus, we go up the chain starting with the first unit you played to the chain, finalizing and resolving all of the pending units on the chain until there are no more units on the chain. Then we finalize any play effects of those units in the order they triggered. Finally, players can react to the most recent item on the chain. If they don’t, that item resolves, and we repeat the process until all items on the chain have resolved.
Relevant rules: 303.2.a.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: What happens when I play Transpositionist’s activated ability choosing an empowered Gangplank, Naval with 6 [M]? Can I play Angler Wyrm?
text:
Q: What happens when I play Transpositionist’s activated ability choosing an empowered Gangplank, Naval with 6 [M]? Can I play Angler Wyrm?
Gangplank being returned to hand will be replaced with him being given +3 [M] this turn. You can play Angler Wyrm from hand with Transpositionist’s activated ability.
Transpositionist returns a unit to hand and then references that unit’s information. If the unit didn’t change zones and it was a legal target as the instruction that targeted it was being processed, the activated ability will reference that unit’s current information. Gangplank, Naval’s current Might as it is referenced is 9 [M], allowing you to play a unit with 9 [M] or less.
Relevant rules: 359.3.e.13., 359.3.e.13.a.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: What happens when I choose an attached Equipment with Orianna, Lady of Clockwork?
text:
Q: What happens when I choose an attached Equipment with Orianna, Lady of Clockwork?
It detaches from the object it is attached to when it becomes a unit. Although its equip ability can be activated and it can be targeted by Weaponmaster triggers, it cannot attach to a unit; nothing will happen when those abilities resolve.
In this rules update we’ve clarified that units cannot be attached to other game objects. If a unit were to be attached to a game object, it would need to stop being a unit first. If a non-unit game object becomes a unit, it will detach from anything it is attached to as it becomes a unit. If an effect would attempt to attach a unit to another game object without making it no longer a unit first, nothing happens.
Relevant rules: 143.5., 435.1.h., 718.6.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: What happens when I choose a gear with Deploy located at a battlefield with Orianna, Lady of Clockwork?
text:
Q: What happens when I choose a gear with Deploy located at a battlefield with Orianna, Lady of Clockwork?
That gear will become a unit-gear when the triggered ability resolves; if their controller doesn’t control that battlefield, they will apply contested status to that battlefield, and a combat or showdown will be staged there in the subsequent cleanup. When the chain clears, that showdown or combat will open.
Relevant rules: 190.3.a., 323.7, 323.8., 323.11., 323.12.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: What happens when I choose another gear with Orianna, Lady of Clockwork and the previous unit-gear stops being a unit? Will its attached Equipment fall off? If
text:
Q: What happens when I choose another gear with Orianna, Lady of Clockwork and the previous unit-gear stops being a unit? Will its attached Equipment fall off? If it’s a deploy gear in base, do I get to move it?
Its attached Equipment will remain attached, and if it is a Deploy gear in base, it will remain in base.
Although units cannot be attached to objects, other objects have no such compunctions. Any attached Equipment that don’t become units will remain attached to the gear even after it stops being a unit. Their Might bonus won’t apply, since the gear doesn’t have a Might, but they will continue to apply their effect text to the gear they are attached to.
The majority of gear with Deploy reference “this battlefield” or “hold here” in such a way that gaining a benefit from base is not possible. That being said, if you want to move it back to a battlefield you can either turn it into a unit again with Orianna, Lady of Clockwork or you can use movement effects that specify moving gear, such as Command: Attack.
Note that there is a small gap between finalizing the Orianna, Lady of Clockwork trigger causing the previous unit-gear to stop being a unit, and the triggered ability resolving and causing the new gear to become a unit. During that gap, neither gear is a unit unless it was already one prior to ever being chosen by Orianna, Lady of Clockwork.
Relevant rules: 137.3.b.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: So how does Neeko, Blending In actually work? When do I choose the legends, do I get three legends per Neeko in my deck, can I add multiple of the same legend t
text:
Q: So how does Neeko, Blending In actually work? When do I choose the legends, do I get three legends per Neeko in my deck, can I add multiple of the same legend to the Legend Zone, do the legends enter ready, and do I need to reveal them to my opponent?
You choose the legends during deck building—at competitive OPL, you must register those legends as part of your deck list, and you can store them with your sideboard. The 3 legends are shared by all Neekos in your deck. You cannot add multiple of the same legend to the Legend Zone. The legends enter ready. You do not need to reveal them to your opponent until they are added to the Legend Zone.
Let’s break down Neeko’s rules text. If your deck (Main Deck or sideboard) has one or more copies of Neeko, Blending In, you pick three legends in addition to your starting Champion Legend. Those 3 legends must be different from each other and from your Champion Legend. Regardless of how many copies of Neeko you have in your deck, you will choose three legends in this way.
When Neeko’s play effect resolves, its controller picks one of the legends chosen during deck building and adds it to their Legend Zone alongside their Champion Legend for as long as Neeko is on the board. If Neeko leaves the board, that legend will also cease to exist. The legends don’t exist in any zone of the game while they’re not in the Legend Zone; they don’t exist at all. That being said, if one or more of those legends are already on the board, a player can’t choose to create additional versions of those legends; they can have at most one legend on the board per legend chosen during deckbuilding. If somehow a player played a fourth Neeko, they would fail to add a legend to their legend zone.
The legends added this way are not tokens. They are legend cards and behave in all ways like normal legends do. If an effect instructs a player to “ready a friendly legend” they can target and ready any legends controlled by them or an ally. If an effect instructs a player to ready “your legend,” that refers to any legend controlled by that player. Such an effect does not target a legend; the legend is chosen as the spell or ability resolves.
Relevant rules: 103.1., 440.2.a., 440.3.b., 440.3.c., 355.10.g.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: What happens when the unit on the board that I Showed Off with Primordial Roar is returned to my hand with Star-Crossed? Do I still deal damage? What about if I
text:
Q: What happens when the unit on the board that I Showed Off with Primordial Roar is returned to my hand with Star-Crossed? Do I still deal damage? What about if I play Lunar Boon and discard the unit from hand?
You still deal damage in both scenarios.
Any referenced characteristics of shown off objects are locked in when you show them off. Regardless of what subsequently happens to them, their information will be able to be checked by the card that showed them off. This also means that giving a unit +[M] or -[M] after showing that unit off will not affect the damage dealt by Primordial Roar; it’s too late by that point.
Relevant rules: 832.1.d.1.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: What counts as reducing a unit’s Might for Ahri, Confident? If I play Discipline on my 1 [M] unit while it’s stunned and located at the same battlefield as an e
text:
Q: What counts as reducing a unit’s Might for Ahri, Confident? If I play Discipline on my 1 [M] unit while it’s stunned and located at the same battlefield as an enemy Leona, Zealot, will I trigger their Ahri, Confident located at that battlefield?
Reducing a unit’s Might means an ability of an object you control causes a unit to receive a -[M] effect. Ahri, Confident will trigger if you Discipline a stunned 1 [M] unit at the same battlefield as an enemy Leona, Zealot.
Although Discipline never causes the unit’s Might to increase, the unit goes from 1 [M] with a -0 [M] effect applied to it, which will not trigger Ahri, Confident, to 3 [M] with a -2 [M] effect applied to it. This change in state triggers Ahri, Confident, the same as a 3 [M] unit being stunned and receiving a -2 [M] effect from Leona, Zealot’s passive ability. Note that this doesn’t work for other cases: if a stunned 3 [M] unit at the same battlefield as an enemy Leona, Zealot has Discipline played on it, that unit will not have a new Might reduction effect applied to it and thus Ahri, Confident will not trigger. Spells, triggered abilities, and activated abilities are easier; if a spell, triggered ability, or activated ability applies non-zero -[M] to a unit, Ahri, Confident will trigger.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: Core Rules Changes
text:
Core Rules Changes
The Unleashed and Vendetta rules updates have laid a relatively stable base for this rules update. We’ve made small changes as necessary, but we have fewer logical holes to patch, and there aren’t any sweeping fixes that need to be implemented in this set. The vast majority of the rules in this update are about new cards and mechanics in the Radiance set.
Now let’s take a look at the rules changes we have in store for Radiance!
—
Radiance Addition: Deploy
Deploy is a new keyword appearing on gear in Radiance. Gear with Deploy enable players to apply localized, battlefield-altering effects.
Gear with Deploy can be played to any battlefield; enemy occupied, friendly, or uncontrolled. However, when an opponent holds a battlefield where you have gear with Deploy, those gear will be killed.
Gear with Deploy remain at their current battlefield so long as they aren’t destroyed. Some effects can move gear with Deploy to other battlefields too!NEW RULE: Deploy keyword added.
Radiance Addition: Disarm
Disarm is a new keyword appearing on units in Radiance.
Disarm is an attack trigger. The first time a unit with Disarm attacks each combat, they will give an enemy unit at their battlefield -1 [M] this turn. If a unit has Disarm 2, they’ll give an enemy unit -2 [M] this turn.
Disarm stacks just like Assault or Shield; meaning if a unit has gained multiple Disarm keywords from different sources, the unit will have one trigger for Disarm with a total of the sum of their Disarm values.NEW RULE: Disarm keyword added.
Radiance Addition: Show Off
Show Off is a new keyword appearing on both units and spells in Radiance.
When you Show Off something, you reveal a card from your hand that matches the requirement, or pick a friendly game object (card or token) on the board with the appropriate characteristics.
Cards with Show Off can reference information from the shown off card or object. That information is locked in when the card or object is shown off, even if it’s referenced later.NEW RULE: Show Off keyword added.
Rules Update: Copy Effects Layer

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: Core Rules Changes
text:
Core Rules Changes (continued)
We saw some confusion on how copy effects work and their placement in the trait-altering layer. In the Radiance rules update, we’ve moved to clarify this by giving copy effects a layer of their own. The first layer is now for copy effects and all subsequent layers (trait-altering, ability-altering, arithmetic) have been shifted down to reflect this change.
Because copy effects only interacted with other copy effects anyway, there was functionally no reason for them to remain in the trait-altering layer. Our hope with this move is that it will be clearer that they only interact with other copy effects. Effects like the Mech tag appended by Experimental Hexplate in the trait-altering layer are not copied by copy effects.NEW RULE: Copy Effects layer added.
Radiance Addition: Copy Game Action
To support and build on this clarification for copy effects, we’ve also added the copy game action to the game actions section.
This section also clarifies how game objects that are created as copies, like the tokens played by Zilean, Time Mage’s replacement effect, work; those game objects don’t have a copy effect applied to them, but are created directly with the copyable traits of the object it is a copy of, as if those were its own printed traits.NEW RULE: Copy game action added.
Radiance Support: Additional Deckbuilding Decisions
Radiance’s Neeko, Blending In adds the first instance of additional choices made during deckbuilding, so we’ve added rules to clarify how those choices are made.NEW RULE: Additional deckbuilding decisions added.
Radiance Support: Equipment Units
Orianna, Lady of Clockwork presents some unique rules scenarios for the game, including what happens to an Equipment that becomes a unit. We decided on the simplest answer: units can’t be attached to other game objects. If an attached game object becomes a unit, it detaches immediately.CLARIFIED RULE: Units cannot be attached to other game objects.CLARIFIED RULE: If an attached non-unit game object becomes a unit, it detaches as it becomes a unit.
Rules Update: Layer Calculations and Object Dependencies
We’ve added rules for layer calculations in an effort to support future interactions and clarify how the layer effects are calculated.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: Core Rules Changes
text:
Core Rules Changes (continued)
When calculating layer effects, each game object is treated individually. If a game object needs to reference information from another game object, the game evaluates that game object’s layer information before returning to calculate the original game object’s information.
If multiple game objects reference information from each other, instead evaluate all of their information simultaneously, layer by layer.NEW RULE: Layer calculation procedure added.
Rules Update: Pick
We’re starting to see the word “pick” appear on cards, which will become even more important when Legacy releases early next year. Pick is the word we’re moving towards for when you make a choice that isn’t a target. We want to make it clear to players that when a card says for you to “choose” something, that means you are targeting what you choose.
When the Legacy rules and templating change is implemented in card text, many cards that currently say “choose” will have their text updated to pick. We are doing some of that work in Radiance. As such, we can also make this clearer in the rules prior to the Legacy rules update.NEW RULE: Pick added.
Rules Update: Conditional Clause Scope
In Vendetta we saw some players understandably confused over the scope of conditional clauses in instruction text.
With the Radiance rules update, we’ve clarified what scope conditional clauses have in a given instruction.NEW RULE: Conditional clauses scope added.
Rules Update: Finalizing Time Actions Scope
We received feedback that cards which referred to “you” when checking if costs were paid or actions were taken was confusing if control of the card is gained by another player. New rules have been added to clarify this.NEW RULE: Instructions of a spell or ability may reference actions taken during Finalization. They will do so by checking whether “you” performed those game actions.NEW RULE: These instructions check whether the game action was performed, not by whom. If another player gains control of the spell or ability after the game action was performed during finalization, it will still be considered true for the purposes of these instructions.
Rules Update: Making New Choices

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: Core Rules Changes
text:
Core Rules Changes (continued)
In the Vendetta rules update we included a model for making new choices as used by cards like Mystic Reversal and Rebuttal. We received feedback that the rules were unclear, and we clarified in the Vendetta FAQ how the interim model would work. Upon review, we found we weren’t entirely satisfied with that implementation. We decided to overhaul how new decisions are made to be simpler and more intuitive.
When making new decisions now, all decisions must be made anew. You can choose to make the same decisions as made previously, but if you’re making new decisions, you can’t go halfway.
Similar to the previous model, all decisions must be legal and valid; however, with this new model, any abilities that trigger on targeting, for example, will trigger again; even if you previously targeted the same unit. It should feel like you’re going through the process of choosing targets all over again.CLARIFIED RULE: Making new choices updated.
Rules Update: Pending Item Target Legality
Players have long wondered whether pending items are legal to target with spells and abilities. It’s very rare that such a case is possible but, like many strange rules interactions in Riftbound, we can blame these few cases on Promising Future. We figured we might as well make it clear: Pending items are not legal targets for spells and abilities.NEW RULE: Pending item target legality clarified.
Rules Update: 2v2 Scoring
The rules for 2v2 scoring were slightly contradictory. In the Vendetta rules update we cleaned them up, and in this rules update they’ve been fully aligned. Specifically, the final point and scoring eligibility special rules now apply only to teams that maintain control of a battlefield during their own or a teammate’s turn, and not during an opponent’s turn.CLARIFIED RULE: 2v2 scoring updated.
Empower Abilities
Vendetta’s Kayle, Justified needed some support from the FAQ. We’ve codified that support with the Radiance rules update.NEW RULE: Game Objects with Empower abilities may have or gain permissions to be Empowered multiple times. Such Game Objects ignore the normal “Play only if not Empowered.” restriction on Empower abilities.Note that this means you can activate the ability even if you’re at your max number of empowered statuses. That is intentional! It just does nothing. That is also intentional.
Negated and Ignored Instructions

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: Core Rules Changes
text:
Core Rules Changes (continued)
Insightful judges and players recognized some strangeness in the rules for linked instructions from the Unleashed rules update, made more apparent by rules added in the Vendetta rules update. In the Vendetta FAQ we clarified how those rules should function, and now we’re codifying that fix into the Radiance rules update.
If an instruction mistargets, that instruction is ignored. If an instruction fails to execute for any other reason, such as it being replaced, skipped, or being impossible to perform, it is negated. Instructions that are ignored will cause any later instructions linked to them to also be ignored. If an instruction is negated, later linked instructions will not be negated; they will still execute if possible. NEW RULE: Negated and ignored instructions added.
Mandatory Requirements and Restrictions
The Vendetta FAQ clarified how Dragon Roost and other mandatory requirements functioned together. We’ve codified that into the rules in the Radiance rules update with extra clarifications. We’ve also codified the concept of a restriction: that being an effect like Perched Grimwyrm’s “Play me only to a battlefield you’ve conquered this turn.” NEW RULE: Mandatory requirements added.NEW RULE: Restrictions added.

source_title: Core Rules: Radiance Patch Notes (Effective October 16, 2026)
title: Legacy Updates
text:
Legacy Updates
As we’ve shared before, we’re preparing a major update to Riftbound rules with Legacy in January. To part the curtain some, this is a massive undertaking—we’re completely reformatting the rules documents to improve their readability as reference for players and judges.
We’re literally starting from the ground up, which will give us room to reduce redundant information, improve ordering, and generally clean up the rules documentation.
To be clear: this is about rewriting the rules to be more readable, and it won’t change how Riftbound’s mechanics actually work.
As always, we do not update the rules of Riftbound or introduce card errata to manage the power level of any card or effect—if we ever need to manage a powerful card, we’ll use other tools.
We’ll release an additional FAQ article after Radiance is released to further clarify remaining points of confusion for players and keep you updated as we learn more.

title: Riftbound: Origins Card Errata
text:
[Download Card Errata]
Hey Riftbounders! We’re sharing a recap of all the card errata for Riftbound: Origins. If you’re new to TCGs or Riftbound is your first TCG, card errata is any updates to card text usually for clarity and sometimes a goof like a typo. If you’re a seasoned TCG player, you might be already diving into the PDF above.
With Origins being our first set, it has more than its fair share of errata, most of it focused on rules clarity and consistency. We expect to issue very little “day zero” errata for future sets. Most of these card errata updates have already been shared through updates in our Core Rules FAQ, so there shouldn’t be too many surprises in there. A few cards that were in the FAQ have received slightly different wordings than previously announced, and there are three cards in this file that weren’t in the FAQ.
This is also a good time to reiterate our philosophy behind card errata. Changes from printed wordings add friction to your gameplay experience, and we don’t issue them lightly. And unlike a digital game, we don’t issue “patches” for game balance reasons. Where printed card wordings created unintended gameplay, were ambiguous about their function, or didn’t quite work in our updated rules, that’s where we’ve chosen to issue errata. The majority of the errata here doesn’t change how these cards work in regular gameplay situations; rather, it clarifies their function and shores it up against edge cases and rules oddities.
We’re heads down on the Riftbound: Origins English Launch (soonTM) and designing many sets to come, so give us some time as we work to update the Card Gallery or add another database resource to note the official language of the cards. Currently, card errata is not planned to be included on any future restocks of Riftbound: Origins or potential localizations of the cards. We’ll keep you all posted if that changes though!
With the recent update to Core Rules along with our Core Rules Patch Notes plus the final piece of the Trinity Force with the Card Errata, the Core Rules FAQ is now obsolete and will be retired on November 4, 2025.
Now, that we have that out of the way, let’s dive into the Riftbound: Origins Card Errata:

title: Vendetta Rules FAQ and Clarifications
text:
Welcome to the FAQ for our first worldwide set release, the Vendetta FAQ! These are questions we’ve gathered from public discussion, from judges across the world, and from members of our own team. We appreciate everyone’s excitement and energy as they discussed the rules update for Vendetta; we hope this FAQ will clarify some points that may have been unclear, or provide answers to common questions you may run into.
One point we want to address directly: as we transition to worldwide release, our FAQs have a delicate timing. We want to gather as many real questions from players and judges as possible, while ensuring players aren’t left in the dark for too long on points that are confusing from the new set. If we release the FAQ too early, we might not catch the things that players are finding confusing; while if we release it too late, players can’t use it to prepare themselves and their decks for upcoming events. For future sets, we’re looking to try different models that might reduce some of the pain points players are feeling with this timing, but for now, we appreciate your patience.
The FAQ is a collection of official rulings. In places where the FAQ differs from the Core Rules Document, the FAQ takes precedence. When a new Core Rules Document is released, it will take precedence over any points that differ from this document.
Throughout this document, we use some specific shorthand to represent symbols in card text. Here’s a short guide:
[E] means “exhaust”
[M] means “Might”
[A] means “one power of any domain”
[C] means “one power of this card’s domain”[C] in Accelerate costs takes on the domain of the Unit, or turns into [A] if the Unit has no domain or multiple domains.[C] in other cases is treated as the corresponding power symbol in all respects, matching how the cards are actually printed—it’s just a design shorthand!

title: What happens when you play Abandon on a spell that was played for its Flow cost?
text:
Q: What happens when you play Abandon on a spell that was played for its Flow cost?
It will be banished when it attempts to leave the chain.
“[T]hen banish it” in flow’s text is short for “if it would leave the chain after becoming a finalized chain item, and leaving the chain wasn’t instructed by its own execution, banish it instead.” Abandon returns the countered card to hand after countering it, but for the purposes of flow’s “then banish it”, this is also leaving the chain. No matter how it happens, as long as the flow spell leaving the chain wasn’t instructed by the execution of the spell itself, it will be banished.
This also applies to effects like Kai’Sa, Evolutionary from Origins, or Fizz, Trickster from Spiritforged.

title: What is the difference between Iascylla and Azir, Sovereign’s uses of “this battlefield”?
text:
Q: What is the difference between Iascylla and Azir, Sovereign’s uses of “this battlefield”?
Iascylla’s delayed trigger refers to the battlefield that she held. Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger refers to the battlefield where he is located.
The difference between these two is that Iascylla has a delayed trigger that references implicit information from her trigger condition: the battlefield where she held. Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger does not reference information from his trigger condition, which purely checks for the event of Azir gaining the attacker designation for the first time each combat. Without that information being checked from the trigger condition, the “this battlefield” in Azir, Sovereign’s attack trigger will be checked when the triggered ability resolves. If it resolves and he is not located at a battlefield, any instructions related to that battlefield will be ignored; otherwise, the battlefield he is currently located at will be used.
Comparatively, when a triggered ability refers to information from its trigger condition, that information is checked when the ability triggers and not on resolution. In the case of Iascylla, her delayed trigger is linked with her hold effect, so the information from the trigger condition of the hold effect can be shared with the delayed trigger.
In future sets, we’ve moved to use more precise templating and wording for abilities like Iascylla’s.
Relevant Rules: 359.3.f.1., 359.3.f.2., 359.3.f.3., 359.3.f.3.b.

title: What happens when I play Moonfall choosing an enemy unit while I control an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened?
text:
Q: What happens when I play Moonfall choosing an enemy unit while I control an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened?
The chosen unit will be given -3 [M]. All other enemy units at the chosen battlefield will be given -2 [M].
Mel, Newly Awakened’s empowered ability is a replacement effect. It replaces the event of a spell or ability you control giving a unit it chooses -[M]. The event it replaces that with is the spell or ability giving an additional -1 [M].
Although Moonfall gives -[M] to multiple units, only one of them is chosen, and thus the only event that is eligible to be replaced is the chosen unit being given -2 [M]. It will be replaced with that unit being given -3 [M]. The events of the other units being given -[M] will not be affected by this replacement effect.
Relevant Rules: 370.1., 370.1.b.

title: What about casting Stupefy while I have an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened?
text:
Q: What about casting Stupefy while I have an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened?
The chosen unit will be given -2 [M], to a minimum of 1 [M]. If it was 2 [M], it will become 1 [M].
In the case of Stupefy, Mel, Newly Awakened replaces the event of Stupefy giving -1 [M] with it giving -2 [M] instead. However, a replacement effect that replaces an event modified by the game effect that generated that event will inherit any of those modifications. In this case, Stupefy modifies the “give -1 [M]” game action and thus event with “to a minimum of 1 [M].” The replaced event will inherit the same modification.
Relevant Rules: 375.

title: Speaking of Mel, can my opponent play Abandon on my spell while I control an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened? What happens?
text:
Q: Speaking of Mel, can my opponent play Abandon on my spell while I control an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened? What happens?
They can play Abandon targeting your spell. On resolution, they will Predict, but nothing else will happen.
Mel, Newly Awakened says “your spells and abilities can’t be countered.” If the spell can’t be countered, Abandon will attempt to counter it and fail, and then it will replace the event of it being put in the Trash with it being returned to its owner’s hand. However, that event never occurred, so there is nothing for the replacement effect to replace. Thus, Abandon will resolve to no effect. The replacement effect only functions within the limit of the resolution of the ability (it’s not a delayed replacement effect that specifies a duration), so even if the spell resolves later, it will go to the Trash as normal.

title: How does it work if I cast Abandon while having an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened but they Rebuttal my spell?
text:
Q: How does it work if I cast Abandon while having an empowered Mel, Newly Awakened but they Rebuttal my spell?
In the case of Rebuttal, gaining control of a spell is not the same thing as countering that spell. Effects that prevent spells being countered don’t prevent their controller from changing. If Rebuttal is played choosing your spell, and they pay [A] during resolution of Rebuttal, they will gain control of it. However, them not paying [A] does not mean the spell will be countered.

title: What new choices can I make when I play Rebuttal and pay [A]?
text:
Q: What new choices can I make when I play Rebuttal and pay [A]?
You can choose any number of targets or modes to make new choices for. The rest remain the same.
If you are remaking choices in this way, any choices you choose not to remake must be legal choices. You can’t choose to have some but not all choices be legal choices. Of course, you can always choose not to make new choices. In that case, any of the current choices will remain in their current state, whether that state is illegal or not.
If a spell has some rules or requirements about the choices made for it, those apply regardless of who controls that spell. For example, if a player plays a spell from face down, they must target game objects located at the battlefield the spell was played from unless the instructions of that spell indicate that a target must be chosen from some other location. Gaining control of such a spell doesn’t change this requirement when making new choices for the spell.
We’ll look at shaping up this section in a future rules update.

title: What happens if I choose to copy an empowered unit when I equip an unempowered unit with Shady Spectacles?
text:
Q: What happens if I choose to copy an empowered unit when I equip an unempowered unit with Shady Spectacles?
Being empowered is a status and is not copyable, thus the equipped unit will remain unempowered.
Shady Spectacles applies a copy effect to the equipped unit. Copy effects copy the printed (or copied, if another copy effect has already been applied) traits of the unit being copied. empowered is a status, a temporary modification, and not part of the printed traits of the card, so it will not be copied by Shady Spectacles. Whatever temporary modifications are applied to the unit as the copy effect is executed on that unit will be unaffected by the copy effect. If the unit has Might increases or decreases, a buff, the empowered status, Temporary, attacker, defender, etc those will remain in place.
Relevant Rules: 477.1.b.1.b.

title: What happens when my opponent’s Akshan, Mischievous steals my equipped Shady Spectacles? What happens if they want to copy Aphelios?
text:
Q: What happens when my opponent’s Akshan, Mischievous steals my equipped Shady Spectacles? What happens if they want to copy Aphelios?
If it was attached to a unit, the equipped unit loses its copy effect. Akshan will then become a copy of a friendly unit of his controller’s choice. If he becomes a copy of Aphelios, his ability will not trigger.
This question deserves a bit more depth. As of the Vendetta rules update, we have clarified how effects like Shady Spectacles and Svellsongur work; they are replacement effects that replace the event of the equipment being attached to a unit with that event plus whatever their effect specifies.
In the case of Svellsongur, the resulting series of events will be:
Attach → Copy the equipped unit’s text to Svellsongur’s effect text for as long as Svellsongur is attached
For Shady Spectacles, the resulting series of events will be:
Attach → Choose a friendly unit and make the equipped unit a copy of that unit for as long as Shady Spectacles is attached
These events are not simultaneous. The attach event executes first, and then whatever event is instructed by the replacement effect is executed. Thus, the answer in the Spiritforged FAQ is no longer true: if you attach Svellsongur to Aphelios, he will not trigger twice. Svellsongur doesn’t have the copied effect text when the attach event executes.
Similarly here, if Akshan nabs Shady Spectacles from an opponent, it will attach and then make him a copy. If his controller chooses to make him a copy of Aphelios, it’s too late by that point for his new triggered ability to see the attachment event; it’s already been completed.
Relevant Rules: 369.1., 370.1.b.1., 370.1.a.2.

title: My Sand Soldier has Shady Spectacles equipped and is a copy of Azir, Ascendent. What happens if I activate the copied Azir’s activatedability before detaching t
text:
Q: My Sand Soldier has Shady Spectacles equipped and is a copy of Azir, Ascendent. What happens if I activate the copied Azir’s activatedability before detaching the Shady Spectacles and then attach them to the same Sand Soldier as a copy of the same Azir, Ascendent? Can I use the activated ability again?
You can.
Each instance of the copied ability is a different ability. The game object remains the same throughout this whole process, so any temporary modifications will remain on the Sand Soldier as it transforms, but the copied rules text is an entirely new instance of the ability. It is the same idea as Svellsongur’s copy of an ability being “refreshed” if Svellsongur is detached and then reattached to the same unit.

title: What happens during combat damage assignment if my 4 [M] unit has both Ki Barrier and Lotus Trap played on it this turn and my opponent has a 4 [M] defender?
text:
Q: What happens during combat damage assignment if my 4 [M] unit has both Ki Barrier and Lotus Trap played on it this turn and my opponent has a 4 [M] defender?
You can order the replacement effects on your unit. If Ki Barrier is first, your unit will take no damage and you will have 3 damage prevention remaining on your unit. If Lotus Trap is first, your unit will take 1 damage and will have no damage prevention remaining on your unit.
With the Vendetta rules update, we’ve streamlined how replacement effects that apply to damage work in combat. Specifically, any replacement effect that would apply to combat damage being dealt will apply instead to combat damage assignment. This was already the case for prevention effects like Ki Barrier or Counterstrike, to prevent several strange edge cases. Now, damage increasing replacement effects will also apply during damage assignment.
Relevant Rules: 465.2.c.4.a., 465.2.c.5.

title: What happens when I discard a Patched Porobot with Hwei, Brooding Painter’s move trigger?
text:
Q: What happens when I discard a Patched Porobot with Hwei, Brooding Painter’s move trigger?
Two triggers will go on the chain, in the order of your choosing. One says “Give me +3 [M] this turn.” while the other says “Ready up to 2 runes.”
Hwei, Brooding Painter says “do the following based on the discarded card's type ...” Unlike our previous reflexive triggers printed on cards that use a similar template (cf Twisted Fate, Gambler), Hwei doesn’t say “do one of the following ...” As long as the card has the appropriate type, you will put the corresponding reflexive trigger on the chain. If somehow there existed a card that was a spell unit gear, you would put three reflexive triggers on the chain when you discard it to Hwei.
Relevant Rules: 387.1.b.

title: If my opponent plays two spells in succession, can I counter the first one with Crumbling Sands?
text:
Q: If my opponent plays two spells in succession, can I counter the first one with Crumbling Sands?
Yes.
Crumbling Sands uses the “finalize” meaning of play, because it checks whether cards have been “played” and isn’t a triggered ability. As long as an opponent (not even necessarily the one who played this spell) has chosen targets, paid costs, checked legality, and completed the process of finalizing another spell, even if that spell was countered, Crumbling Sands can counter a spell. That means it can counter the first spell played, as long as another spell was played by an opponent after that one.
Relevant Rules: 419.4.b.

title: When can I react to my opponent playing Fallen Feline to a battlefield? And how does naming a card work?
text:
Q: When can I react to my opponent playing Fallen Feline to a battlefield? And how does naming a card work?
You can react to the play effect of Fallen Feline, before they’ve named a spell.
Fallen Feline’s play effect instructs its controller to name a spell. This occurs on resolution of the triggered ability. If Fallen Feline is played to a battlefield, as soon as the ability resolves, opponents cannot play spells with that name. Meaning spells by that name can not be put onto a chain. Any spells already on the chain when Fallen Feline’s ability resolves will be unaffected. However, by the time you know the chosen spell it’s too late to play that spell.
Naming a card or tag has new rules with the Vendetta rules update. When naming something in this way, the overarching rule that applies to all naming is that you can’t name something that doesn’t exist in Riftbound. You can’t name the “Locke” tag, the “totem” type, nor a card named “Lingering Tentacles,” because none of those has been printed on cards or tokens in Riftbound.
However, you can name a card using information that uniquely identifies it. That information could be its name, but it could just as well be something like “the [3] spell with Flow that makes tentacles” or “the red Kai’Sa” or “Illaoi.” As long as there is no ambiguity as to what card is being named, a player can use whatever method is clear to their opponents and teammates. You can’t name a card by saying just “Kai’Sa” if there are two or more cards that could be identified in that way—you won’t have named a card if that’s all you say.
Relevant Rules: 761., 761.1., 761.2., 762., 762.1., 762.2.

title: If I disempower a Kayle, Justified who has been empowered 3 times, does she lose all of her empowered statuses?
text:
Q: If I disempower a Kayle, Justified who has been empowered 3 times, does she lose all of her empowered statuses?
No. She will lose one of her empowered statuses.
For every Riftbound card other than Kayle, empowered is a binary status. They are either empowered or not. Kayle utilizes the golden rule “Card text supersedes rules text” to overcome this and be able to escape the normal bounds of what the empowered status means. On Kayle, empowered isn’t a binary status but a stacking status; she can have up to 3 empowered statuses. When Kayle is disempowered, the disempower action attempts to remove the empowered status. If she only has one empowered status, great, it’s gone. If she has more than one empowered status, the disempower action will remove one of the empowered statuses from Kayle.

title: But can I activate Kayle’s empower ability even if she’s already empowered?
text:
Q: But can I activate Kayle’s empower ability even if she’s already empowered?
Yes.
Kayle’s empower ability can be activated any number of times. If she has less than 3 empowered statuses, she will become empowered. If she has 3 empowered statuses, the ability can still be activated but nothing will happen when the ability resolves.

title: What happens if my opponent plays Flash on their Akali, Silent that’s currently in combat after I play Star-Crossed targeting her?
text:
Q: What happens if my opponent plays Flash on their Akali, Silent that’s currently in combat after I play Star-Crossed targeting her?
Akali will be unaffected by Star Crossed as it resolves.
Akali, Silent is what the rules refer to as “untargetable” for enemy spells and abilities when she isn’t in combat; meaning she is not a legal target for them. Enemy spells and abilities being played when she’s untargetable can’t choose her. If she becomes untargetable after she’s already been chosen by an effect and retains it as that effect begins to resolve, it will “mistarget” her. She will be unaffected by any of the spell or ability’s instructions. If an instruction chooses only her, that instruction will be ignored.
Relevant Rules: 757.1., 758., 758.1.

title: I have a Ravenbloom Student on the board and I haven’t played any spells this turn. What happens when I play Rebuttal targeting my opponent’s Stupefy and pay [A
text:
Q: I have a Ravenbloom Student on the board and I haven’t played any spells this turn. What happens when I play Rebuttal targeting my opponent’s Stupefy and pay [A] on resolution? After everything resolves, how much will Battering Ram cost? Will my opponent’s Legion abilities be active?
Ravenbloom Student will trigger twice, Battering Ram will cost [4], and your opponent’s Legion abilities will be active.
Ravenbloom Student’s triggered ability checks whether a spell that you control resolves. You gained control of the Stupefy, and it resolved, so you will have triggered Ravenbloom Student’s ability. Battering Ram and Legion, on the other hand, check whether cards were finalized. Although you gained control of Stupefy, you did not finalize it; you got it after it was already finalized by your opponent. Thus, your opponent’s Legion abilities will be active, and Battering Ram will only receive a [1] Energy discount.
Relevant Rules: 419.4., 419.4.a., 419.4.b.

title: What happens when I conquer with Swain, Visionary, if I’ve only played a Patched Porobot and Stupefy this turn?
text:
Q: What happens when I conquer with Swain, Visionary, if I’ve only played a Patched Porobot and Stupefy this turn?
You will score 2 points total. 1 from conquering, 1 from Swain.
Swain only checks whether you’ve played a non-token unit, a non-token gear, and a spell. Checks like that do not care whether they were satisfied by multiple cards or a single card relevant to the trigger conditions.

title: What happens when my opponent plays Switcheroo on their 2 [M] unit and my empowered Gangplank, Naval?
text:
Q: What happens when my opponent plays Switcheroo on their 2 [M] unit and my empowered Gangplank, Naval?
Gangplank, Naval will replace his Might being lowered with him being given +3 [M] this turn.
Swap calculates the difference in Might and generates two effects: an increase, and a decrease. When a swap effect is applied to two units’ Mights, it gives those units +[M] and -[M] respective to who has the higher Might.
Under the hood, Gangplank’s replacement effect sees the event of him being given -[M] and replaces it with him being given +3 [M] this turn instead. The event of the other unit being given +[M] is unaffected by Gangplank’s replacement effect. By the time we apply the replacement effect, the difference between the two units has been calculated. In the example with the 2 [M] unit, the final Mights of the two units will be 2 [M] → 6 [M], and 6 [M] → 9 [M].
The way this works is not immediately obvious based on how the swap game action rules are written. We will clarify this in a future rules update.
Note that this logic also applies to Mel, Newly Awakened and Switcheroo.

title: What happens when my empowered Gangplank, Naval is moved by my opponent’s Blast Cone’s play effect and they exhaust Blast Cone to stun Gangplank? Will he be stu
text:
Q: What happens when my empowered Gangplank, Naval is moved by my opponent’s Blast Cone’s play effect and they exhaust Blast Cone to stun Gangplank? Will he be stunned? What happens if I then play Back Off choosing my Gangplank? Will he get +3 [M] this turn?
Blast Cone will stun Gangplank. If you play Back Off choosing your stunned Gangplank, he will not receive +3 [M] this turn.
Blast Cone’s triggered ability that stuns units doesn’t choose them, so Gangplank’s replacement effect can’t apply to that event. Back Off played on a stunned Gangplank does not actually perform the stun game action, because Gangplank is already stunned. It’s legal to play Back Off, but the instruction will be negated. In order for Gangplank’s replacement effect to replace an event of him being stunned, the stun game action must actually be performed. Similarly, if an effect that said “Friendly units can’t be stunned” were active with a friendly empowered Gangplank, Naval is on the board, a stun effect that is played choosing Gangplank wouldn’t generate an event that Gangplank could replace, because no stun game action is performed.
Relevant Rules: 423.1.a.1.

title: What happens if I play Stupefy on my 1 [M] empowered Gangplank, Naval? Will he get +3 [M] this turn?
text:
Q: What happens if I play Stupefy on my 1 [M] empowered Gangplank, Naval? Will he get +3 [M] this turn?
He will not.
In order for his replacement effect to apply, the event of him being given -[M] must occur. In the case of Stupefy played on a 1 [M] unit, no -[M] is given; it is snapshot to -0 [M]. Thus, there is no suitable event for Gangplank’s replacement effect to replace.
Relevant Rules: 477.3.b.

title: What happens when my opponent plays Hidden Blade targeting my Akali, Deadly Weapon in reaction to her move trigger? Will it still deal damage to the chosen unit
text:
Q: What happens when my opponent plays Hidden Blade targeting my Akali, Deadly Weapon in reaction to her move trigger? Will it still deal damage to the chosen unit?
It will.
Akali is another case where her ability refers to information implicit to its own trigger condition, similar to Iascylla. Akali’s “battlefield I moved to or from” doesn’t require her to be on the board in order for us to be able to identify it, nor does it reference information about her current state. Even if she leaves the board, that information was checked when her ability triggered, and it is still available to us on resolution.
Relevant Rules: 359.3.f.3.

title: Can I activate an empowered Heimerdinger, Inventor to ready 2 gear if my Jayce, Defender of Tomorrow legend isn’t empowered? What about if my Heimerdinger isn’t
text:
Q: Can I activate an empowered Heimerdinger, Inventor to ready 2 gear if my Jayce, Defender of Tomorrow legend isn’t empowered? What about if my Heimerdinger isn’t empowered?
You can activate Heimerdinger’s ability if he is empowered, regardless of the empowered status of Jayce, Defender of Tomorrow.
There is a bit of a trick here, in that there are two important details to this question relating to dependent keywords:
First is that a dependent keyword (the kind of ability that [Level][>] or [Empowered][>] are when they appear with the arrow) includes the whole of the ability, including the dependent ability. They’re all one object, so to speak.
Second is that a dependent keyword’s dependent ability still exists and can be referenced while it is inactive—that is, if its condition isn’t met. In this case, the condition is that the source of the ability is empowered.
Heimerdinger gains all activated abilities that have the [E] symbol in their cost, and he gains the entire ability, restrictions, costs, dependent keywords and all. In effect, Defender of Tomorrow’s ability that Heimerdinger is gaining is the whole line that says:
[Empowered][>] [1], [E]: Ready 2 gear.
Heimerdinger can gain this ability even if Defender of Tomorrow isn’t empowered because of that second point we made previously.
The key rule for this case is 727.1.b.1., which reads:
The Dependent Ability is present on the card for the sake of reference or evaluation until the Condition is met.
This means that the ability isn’t active and its text isn’t being processed yet, but other effects can reference or evaluate its text before the condition is met. Heimerdinger, Inventor is exactly one such effect.
Relevant Rules: 727.1., 727.1.b., 727.1.b.1.

title: What card does Astral Heron’s triggered ability discount?
text:
Q: What card does Astral Heron’s triggered ability discount?
It discounts the next card played (added to the chain and queued for finalization) this turn after the ability resolves.
Astral Heron has received an erratum to update its wording: “When you play your first card each turn, if I'm at a battlefield, the next card you play this turn costs [2][A][A] less.”

title: What happens when I play Temporal Breach targeting my Elder Dragon in base and pay [A][A] for Dragon Roost while playing Elder Dragon? Will it be played to base
text:
Q: What happens when I play Temporal Breach targeting my Elder Dragon in base and pay [A][A] for Dragon Roost while playing Elder Dragon? Will it be played to base or to Dragon Roost?
You can choose which of those two locations you want to play it to.
In general, there are not many cases where we have this kind of competing instruction: one effect that tells you to play a unit to one location, and one that tells you to play it to another. That being said, when they do arise with contradictory requirements, the precedent from other areas of the rules is that the player chooses one of those requirements and ignores all others.
Note that this only applies to mandatory positive requirements, ones that specify a location or method without also preventing the action from being performed to other locations or with other methods and that aren’t optional. For example, an effect like Perched Grimwyrm’s passive ability is a restriction on playing that unit to any location other than a battlefield you’ve conquered this turn. Rockfall Path’s passive ability is a restriction on playing units to Rockfall Path. If you’ve conquered only Rockfall Path this turn, you can’t play Perched Grimwyrm at all, because those two restrictions are contradictory.
In this case, the contradictory requirements don’t directly prohibit the playing of these units to other locations, so we can choose one of the contradictory requirements and ignore the rest.

title: What happens when I play Perched Grimwyrm while I haven’t conquered Dragon Roost this turn? Can I pay [A][A] and play it to Dragon Roost? What if I’ve conquered
text:
Q: What happens when I play Perched Grimwyrm while I haven’t conquered Dragon Roost this turn? Can I pay [A][A] and play it to Dragon Roost? What if I’ve conquered another battlefield this turn?
You cannot.
In Riftbound, “can’t” beats “can.” Perched Grimwyrm’s effect is a “can’t,” as in it can’t be played to any location but to a battlefield you’ve conquered this turn. Dragon Roost’s ability tries to give the Grimwyrm permission to be played to the Roost, but that can’t overcome Perched Grimwyrm’s own restriction. If you have no ability to play Perched Grimwyrm to Dragon Roost after paying for it, you will not be able to finalize Perched Grimwyrm at all. The actions taken as part of playing Perched Grimwyrm will be undone and it will be returned to the zone it was played from.
This is true even if you’ve conquered another battlefield this turn. If you have the ability, you can play Perched Grimwyrm to that battlefield without paying the additional cost of Dragon Roost, but you can’t play it to Dragon Roost itself unless you’ve conquered it.
Sharp eyed readers may remember that Baron Nashor doesn’t work this way. He enters at the Baron Pit regardless of effects preventing him from being played to battlefields. The reason for this is that Baron Nashor’s passive ability generates a delayed replacement effect, the one that reads “I enter there.” This replacement effect replaces the event of him entering to any other location with him entering to the Baron Pit. The replacement effect gets around effects like Mageseeker Warden which limit where you can play units. However, Dragon Roost is not written as a replacement effect. It tells you where to play the dragon you’ve paid the additional cost for, but it doesn’t specify how that dragon enters the board. Therefore it is a permission on play location, but not a replacement effect.
Relevant Rules: 054.2., 369.3.

title: Can I disempower my Ambessa, Matriarch of War with Profiteer to empower my Kayle? Do I control my own legend?
text:
Q: Can I disempower my Ambessa, Matriarch of War with Profiteer to empower my Kayle? Do I control my own legend?
Yes, you can disempower Ambessa, Matriarch of War with Profiteer. And yes, you control your own legend.
We don’t typically consider the possibility that any player controls a legend, because control of legends cannot change, but you do indeed control your own legend.

title: What happens if I play Dragon Form on a unit that has -1 [M] from Stupefy applied to it? Will my Fiora, Grand Duelist trigger? Is there a moment where my unit b
text:
Q: What happens if I play Dragon Form on a unit that has -1 [M] from Stupefy applied to it? Will my Fiora, Grand Duelist trigger? Is there a moment where my unit becomes 5 [M] before the -1 [M] from Stupefy brings it down to 4 [M]?
She will not trigger.
Although Dragon Form sets the base Might of a unit to 5 [M], it does so via layers. Layers are evaluated when the effect is applied and their evaluation includes all existing applied layer alterations. We process layers in order, starting from the Trait-Altering layer (where this base Might setting effect is applied), proceeding to the Ability-Altering layer (not part of this example), and proceeding to the Arithmetic layer (where Stupefy’s -1 [M] is applied), but this process happens instantaneously; there is no window while evaluating layers for the unit to see itself become 5 [M] and then go down to 4 [M]. As soon as the effect of Dragon Form is applied, the unit is 4 [M].
As a side note, Might is one of the traits that is managed in the Trait-Altering layer, and it is one of the copyable traits that copy effects can replace or add to.

title: What happens when I play Hostile Takeover gaining control of my opponent’s ready unit, move it to base, and then play Temporal Breach choosing it? Where will th
text:
Q: What happens when I play Hostile Takeover gaining control of my opponent’s ready unit, move it to base, and then play Temporal Breach choosing it? Where will the unit go?
The unit will remain in Banishment.
Units cannot be played to a base of a player other than their own controller under any circumstances. Because the owner of the unit is the one being instructed to play the unit, and the location they are being instructed to play it to is a base other than their own, it isn’t possible to play the unit. During the check legality step of finalization, the unit will be returned to banishment from the chain and all actions taken will be undone.

title: My 11 Might Renekton, Brute is disempowered by my own Profiteer. What happens when my opponent plays Stupefy choosing him? Will his ability trigger? What happen
text:
Q: My 11 Might Renekton, Brute is disempowered by my own Profiteer. What happens when my opponent plays Stupefy choosing him? Will his ability trigger? What happens if instead I activated his ability?
Renekton’s ability will not trigger in either scenario.
In order to “become 10 or more,” his Might would have to have previously been less than 10. “10 or more” is a state, and Renekton’s triggered ability checks for the event of him achieving that state. If he maintains that state, regardless of how his Might changes, he will not “become” that state.

title: What happens when I play Icathian Rain choosing a Recruit at Heisho, Shell of the World once and Irelia, Fervent in base five times? How many times do I pay for
text:
Q: What happens when I play Icathian Rain choosing a Recruit at Heisho, Shell of the World once and Irelia, Fervent in base five times? How many times do I pay for deflect?
You will not pay for deflect.
While your spell or ability chooses a unit at Heisho, Shell of the World, you ignore deflect while paying for the spell. Ignore, in this context, means you treat deflect on the specified units as being inactive, like it’s turned off temporarily. In the case of Heisho, it doesn’t specify any units whose deflect to ignore, so you ignore all instances of deflect on units.
This only applies to the specified spell or ability. You can’t play a spell or ability choosing a unit at Heisho, and then play another one choosing a unit at another location and not at Heisho and still ignore deflect. Only while at least one target of the spell or ability is a unit located at Heisho do you ignore deflect while paying costs for that spell or ability.
Relevant Rules: 766., 767.

title: What happens when I play Hextech Ray on an Elder Dragon while Imperial Decree’s delayed trigger is active and I have an Immortal Phoenix in the Trash? Can I pla
text:
Q: What happens when I play Hextech Ray on an Elder Dragon while Imperial Decree’s delayed trigger is active and I have an Immortal Phoenix in the Trash? Can I play Immortal Phoenix from the Trash?
You can.
Per the current rules, there is nothing that would stop Imperial Decree’s delayed trigger from triggering Immortal Phoenix. It is a triggered ability generated by a spell; it is attributed a kill action, and thus the spell that generated it will also be attributed the same kill action. The owner of Imperial Decree is the controller of the delayed triggered ability; the player responsible for the kill action is the one who controls the ability; and that same player is the owner of Immortal Phoenix in the Trash. Thus all three conditions for Immortal Phoenix triggering are complete, and it will trigger.

title: If I play Ride the Wind targeting my unit at Vilemaw’s Lair and attempt to move them to base, what happens?
text:
Q: If I play Ride the Wind targeting my unit at Vilemaw’s Lair and attempt to move them to base, what happens?
They will be readied.
This is a rules quirk that players and judges identified as a result of a small additional rule added in the Vendetta rules update. We’re going to give some clarity to this that will resolve this issue, but if you don’t understand the conversation or why it is necessary, don’t worry. This isn’t an actual change to how we’ve been interpreting and ruling cards, but smoothing out a bug.
In short, the linked instructions rules are too expansive currently on what qualifies as an “ignored” instruction. To clarify this definition: an ignored instruction is one that wasn’t performed as part of the execution of a spell or ability’s instructions because it mistargeted (i.e. because the targeted object wasn’t a legal target on resolution). This is a case where, for example, you play Hidden Blade choosing an enemy unit and they play Star-Crossed in reaction, returning their unit to hand. When Hidden Blade resolves, the unit isn’t on the board, so we ignore the “Its controller draws 2.” instruction. Alternatively, if Hidden Blade is given the Repeat keyword by the Academy and both executions target the same unit, this is the reason why the unit’s controller doesn’t draw 4 cards.
An instruction is not ignored if an ability, effect, or circumstance of the game prevents it from occurring. This could take the form of a replacement effect that replaces the event of the instruction with something else, it could take the form of an ability like Vilemaw’s Lair that says “Units can’t move from here to base.” or it could take the form of a game action like Buff or Ready being performed on a unit that already has the appropriate state. It could even take the form of a unit, gear, or spell no longer being in an appropriate zone as long as the instruction doesn’t target those objects. The instruction in these cases isn’t ignored, but instead negated. A negated instruction has its effects skipped, replaced, or prevented. A negated instruction will not cause any linked instructions to be ignored unless those instructions refer specifically to the action being performed.
Some examples:

title: If I play Ride the Wind targeting my unit at Vilemaw’s Lair and attempt to move them to base, what happens?
text:
If I play Ride the Wind targeting my unit at Vilemaw’s Lair and attempt to move them to base, what happens? (continued)
If a unit at a battlefield says “I can’t be killed.” and a player plays Hidden Blade choosing that unit, the unit’s controller will still draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (The instruction was negated and not ignored, so the linked instruction will still execute.)
If a unit at a battlefield is chosen by Hidden Blade and in reaction its controller plays Flash moving it to base, that unit’s controller will not draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (The instruction was ignored, so any linked instructions will be ignored.)
If a unit at a battlefield is chosen by Hidden Blade and in reaction its controller plays Zhonya’s Hourglass, that unit’s controller will draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (The unit is on the board and can have its information checked, and the instruction was negated and not ignored.)
If a unit at a battlefield has been affected by Smite previously this turn and it is chosen by Hidden Blade, that unit’s controller will not draw 2 on resolution of Hidden Blade. (Although the instruction is executed, the unit is not on the board to have its information checked. Additionally, the unit was moved to a non-board zone by an effect other than Hidden Blade and thus no longer has a controller that Hidden Blade can reference.)

title: Unleashed Rules FAQ and Clarifications
text:
We are aware that Unleashed’s core rules updates caused consternation among some players and judges. This set’s updates had several mitigating factors which came together and impacted how we approached it, among them were changes to our internal processes which were necessary towards us improving our systems for generating and updating our rules documents. We are also improving how we present these changes and communicate them to players and judges. Today’s content will hopefully resolve many of the issues and sources of confusion for the community.
While the updates we released for Unleashed were substantive, it was a first step of a transitional period for Riftbound’s rules and templating, as they are dependent on future sets. Given this limitation, we are going to focus on clarifying points of confusion under the current structures. There will be things which will remain awkward in the meantime and we appreciate everyone’s patience as we forge ahead together.
We’ll start this FAQ out by clearing up a few points that were left confusing from the rules update—if you’re not deeply invested in the rules and just want to see answers to common questions, skip down to the Frequently Asked Questions section in the latter half of the document. For any points that differ between this document and the Core Rules Document, this document will take precedence. When the next rules update is published, this document will become obsolete. You can always visit the Rules Hub to find the current rules documents for Riftbound.
Throughout this document, we use some specific shorthand to represent symbols in card text. Here’s a short guide:
[E] means “exhaust”
[M] means “Might”
[A] means “one power of any domain”
[C] means “one power of this card’s domain”[C] in Accelerate costs takes on the domain of the unit, or turns into [A] if the unit has no domain or multiple domains.[C] in other cases is treated as the corresponding power symbol in all respects, matching how the cards are actually printed—it’s just a design shorthand!

title: Triggered Abilities
text:
Triggered Abilities
We’ll start with the most significant and contextual rules change in this update. As of our third rules update, triggered abilities have been changed in their structure: rather than a one clause condition and a potentially multi-clause effect, there are now multiple pieces that need to be considered when putting a triggered ability on the chain and finalizing it. The easiest way to think about these is shifting where the effect and condition split into two components of the triggered ability: instead of at the first comma, it now depends on how the triggered ability is templated. Triggered abilities will have one or more of the following four items in sequence:
A trigger condition
A conditional statement next to the trigger condition
A “you may” that appears next to the conditional statement
A cost within instruction next to the “you may”
We can best see this in the example of Piltover Enforcer, the Vi Legend from Unleashed: “[When you conquer], [if you assigned 3 or more excess damage], [you may] [exhaust me to] ready a unit.” This ability contains all four elements in the sequence.
A trigger condition: “When you conquer”
Extra conditional: “If you assigned 3 or more excess damage,”
A “you may” that appears next to the conditional: “You may,” - this indicates the decision of whether or not to place the ability on the chain
A cost within instruction next to the “you may”: “Exhaust me to...” - is the cost within instructions that becomes the base cost of the triggered ability.
We can imagine splitting this ability into two sections: the part including this sequence and the part after it:
Before
After
The second section only becomes a finalized chain item when the first section is fulfilled by the process of finalization; that being the process by which players make choices, pay costs, and check legality for cards and abilities. When the trigger condition and extra conditional are fulfilled and the player decides to place it on the chain, it will become a pending chain item and be queued for finalization. If its controller chooses a legal target and pays the cost during the subsequent finalization, the second section will become a finalized chain item. All it says on the chain is “Ready a unit,” where the unit is the one chosen during finalization.

title: Triggered Abilities
text:
Triggered Abilities (continued)
Triggered abilities, however, don’t need to contain all of the above elements in order for the sequence to follow these rules, as long as the elements that do appear are where they would be based on our understanding of the above sequence.
Let’s look at a few examples:
Sona, Harmonious reads “At the end of your turn, if I'm at a battlefield, ready up to 4 friendly runes.” “If I’m at a battlefield,” appears where we would expect it to based on the sequence described above, so it is part of the condition and not the effect. The ability can be split into “At the end of your turn, if I’m at a battlefield,” and “ready up to 4 runes.”
Disarming Rake reads “When you play me, you may kill a gear.” The “you may” appears here where we would expect it to based on the sequence above, so it is the choice of whether or not to place the ability on the chain, and not part of the effect itself. The ability can be split into “When you play me, you may” and “kill a gear.”
Ekko, Recurrent reads, “[Deathknell][>] Recycle me to ready your runes.” Deathknell is functionally short for “When I die, ...” We can translate this to our sequence as “When I die, recycle me to ready your runes.” “Recycle me to” is a cost within instructions that appears where we would expect it to based on our sequence, so it becomes the base cost of the ability when it is placed on the chain and is not part of the effect. The ability can be split into “When I die, recycle me to” and “ready your runes.”
Any of these elements that appear later in the ability than where you would expect based on the sequence do not function in this way.
Loose Cannon, the Jinx Legend, reads “At the start of your Beginning Phase, draw 1 if you have one or fewer cards in your hand.” The conditional statement “if you have one or fewer cards in your hand,” does not appear where we would expect in the sequence described above, so it is considered part of the effect and not the condition. This ability can be split into “At the start of your Beginning Phase,” and “draw 1 if you have one of fewer cards in your hand.”

title: Triggered Abilities
text:
Triggered Abilities (continued)
Ornn, Blacksmith reads “When you play me or when I hold, look at the top 4 cards of your Main Deck. You may reveal a gear from among them and draw it. Then recycle the rest.” The “you may” here doesn’t appear in the appropriate place to be part of the sequence, so it is not a decision made when the ability triggers and instead is made when ability resolves. This ability can be split into “When you play me or when I hold,” and “look at the top 4 cards of your Main Deck. You may reveal a gear from among them and draw it. Then recycle the rest.”
Insightful Investigator reads “When you play me, choose an opponent. They reveal their hand. You may pay 2 XP to choose a card from their hand. If you do, they discard that card and draw 1.” Here we see the final example, where the ability contains a cost within instructions that does not fall where we would expect it to be for the sequence. This cost within instructions is paid on resolution and not as the base cost of the triggered ability. The ability can be split into “When you play me,” and “Choose an opponent. They reveal their hand. You may pay 2 XP to choose a card from their hand. If you do, they discard that card and draw 1.” The second part of the ability is all one chain item—it resolves it one go, and cannot be reacted to partway through resolution.
One notable effect of this change is that we see a larger difference between two previously similar templates: costs within instructions (“[do X] to [do Y]”) and “if you do” templates. The two templates had some overlap, in that they asked players to perform an action in order to get an effect. The templates, however, were still functionally different before this rules update. Costs don’t care if the game action being performed is replaced, as long as an attempt was made to perform the action.
“If you do” templating is more particular, as seen in cards like Jayce, Man of Progress whose triggered ability begins with, “When you play me, you may kill a friendly gear. If you do, ...” Killing the friendly gear in this case is not a cost for the ability, but a game action that a later instruction checks. If the game action is not performed or is replaced, the later instruction will not have its condition fulfilled - the player didn’t “do” it, so “if you do” is not true.

title: Triggered Abilities
text:
Triggered Abilities (continued)
While this was always the case, now there is even more differentiation, as “if you do” templating isn’t a cost within instructions and therefore cannot be the base cost of the triggered ability. Even if resources are instructed to be spent, as in the case of Draven, Vanquisher (RIP), who reads “When I attack or defend, you may pay [C]. If you do, ...” those resources are not a cost and are paid on resolution of the ability and not finalization.

title: Control of Battlefields and Showdowns
text:
Control of Battlefields and Showdowns
Two areas that were unclear in the rules update were control of battlefields and when Showdowns open. How battlefield control is managed is contradictory in two places: in the control rules under rule 187.4.c., and in the cleanup rules under rule 323.6. To clarify this: rule 323.6. should read, “Players lose control of any controlled battlefields without their Units occupying them if the turn is in an open state and there is no Showdown or Combat ongoing there.” This was our intent, as seen in the patch notes, and the wording of rule 323.6 lagged behind it.
(OLD) 4. If the turn is in an Open State, Battlefields with no Units occupying them and no Showdown or Combat ongoing become Uncontrolled.
(NEW) 4. Players lose control of any controlled Battlefields without their Units occupying them if the turn is in an open state and there is no Showdown or Combat ongoing there.
